**fusion category** is a finite semisimple tensor category. In particular the
unit of a fusion category is simple, whereas a multifusion unit may split.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over $k$. A **finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category** is a finite semisimple $k$-linear category $\mathcal M$ in the sense of [[def-semisimple-object-and-semisimple-abelian-category]], a bilinear action functor $\odot:\mathcal M\times\mathcal C\to\mathcal M$, and natural isomorphisms
$$\alpha_{m,X,Y}:(m\odot X)\odot Y\longrightarrow m\odot(X\otimes Y),\qquad \rho_m:m\odot\mathbf1\longrightarrow m,$$
which satisfy the module pentagon and triangle equations obtained from the associator and unitors of $\mathcal C$. The left-action convention is defined by reversing the order of the action factors.

A **module functor** $F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal N$ is a linear functor with natural action comparisons $F(m\odot X)\cong F(m)\odot X$ satisfying the module associativity and unit equations. A **module-natural transformation** is a natural transformation commuting with those comparisons. These objects, functors, and transformations form a 2-category denoted $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C)$ once its composition and monoidal product are specified.

This definition alone does not assert that there are finitely many equivalence classes of simple module categories, nor that $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C)$ is a fusion 2-category.

derivations.claim: On the real vector space with orthonormal basis $b_i=[X_i]$, rigidity gives Frobenius reciprocity $N_{ij}^k=N_{i^*k}^j=N_{kj^*}^i$, and $N_{ij}^0=\delta_{j,i^*}$. Indeed the adjunctions $\operatorname{Hom}(X_i\otimes X_j,X_k)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(X_j,X_i^*\otimes X_k)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(X_i\otimes X_j,X_k)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(X_i,X_k\otimes X_j^*)$ give the first equalities by dimensions; simplicity of the unit gives the second. Left and right multiplication matrices $L_i,R_i$ therefore have transposes $L_{i^*},R_{i^*}$, respectively, and $L_iR_j=R_jL_i$ by associativity. The matrix $S=\sum_i L_i$ is real symmetric and strictly positive entrywise: for any $a,b$, the nonzero object $X_b\otimes X_a^*$ has a simple summand $X_i$, and reciprocity then gives $N_{ia}^b>0$. The object is nonzero because tensoring by a nonzero rigid object is faithful: the unit is a summand of its dual times itself, so a zero tensor product would force the other factor to be zero.

Here is the required positive-matrix argument without an unproved Perron theorem. A real symmetric strictly positive matrix $T$ has a largest eigenvalue $\lambda$ by the finite-dimensional spectral theorem, equivalently the maximum of $v^tTv$ on the real unit sphere. Replacing a maximizing vector by its coordinatewise absolute value cannot decrease this expression; take a nonnegative maximizer $v$. The equation $Tv=\lambda v$ implies $\lambda>0$ and every coordinate of $v$ is positive. Every maximizing vector has coordinates of one sign: if both signs occur, taking absolute values strictly increases its quadratic form because every cross entry is positive. Hence the top eigenspace is one-dimensional, for an independent top eigenvector could be chosen orthogonal to $v$ and would necessarily have both signs. Apply this to $S$ and normalize its positive top eigenvector $v$ by $v_0=1$.

Since $R_i$ commutes with $S$, $R_iv=d_iv$ for a scalar $d_i$; it is positive because $R_i$ is nonzero and nonnegative and $v$ is strictly positive. Transposition and the scalar product give $d_i\langle v,v\rangle=\langle v,R_iv\rangle=\langle R_{i^*}v,v\rangle=d_{i^*}\langle v,v\rangle$. The coefficient of $b_0$ in $v b_i$ is $v_{i^*}$, so $d_i=v_{i^*}=v_i$. Right multiplication by a product now gives $d_id_j=\sum_kN_{ij}^kd_k$, and $R_0=1$ gives $d_0=1$. These numbers are fixed by the fusion data, since $S$ and the normalization of its unique positive top eigenvector are fixed. Writing $\Omega=\sum_i d_i b_i=v$, we have $\Omega b_i=d_i\Omega$ and therefore $\Omega^2=D\Omega$ for $D=\sum_i d_i^2$.

For a module category let $A_i$ have entry $(b,a)$ equal to $n_{ai}^b$. Adjunction for the action, obtained by applying its associator to the evaluation and coevaluation of $X_i$, gives $\operatorname{Hom}(m_a\odot X_i,m_b)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(m_a,m_b\odot X_i^*)$, hence $A_i^t=A_{i^*}$. The matrices represent the fusion ring in the opposite order, which does not affect the equation for the square of a single element. Thus $B=\sum_i d_iA_i$ is symmetric, has nonnegative entries, satisfies $B^2=DB$, and has diagonal entries at least one since $A_0=1$. If the category is indecomposable, $B$ is strictly positive: the undirected graph joining simples whenever some $A_i$ has a positive connecting entry is connected, since its connected components are exactly action-stable summands. A path from $a$ to $b$ gives a positive entry in the product of its action matrices. Associativity expands that product as a nonnegative integer sum of the $A_i$, so some $A_i$ already connects $a$ to $b$.

Every eigenvalue of symmetric $B$ is either $0$ or $D$, by $B^2=DB$. In the indecomposable case strict positivity and step 2.1 make its top eigenspace one-dimensional; since $B\ne0$, its nonzero eigenvalue is $D$ and it has rank one. Thus $r\le\operatorname{tr}B=D$, as each of its $r$ diagonal entries is at least one. For the multiplicity bound in any module category, no indecomposability is needed: the same polynomial identity and symmetry show that the operator norm of $B$ is $D$, so $0\le d_i(A_i)_{ba}\le B_{ba}\le D$ by applying the norm inequality to the unit coordinate vectors. Each entry is therefore a nonnegative integer bounded by $D/d_i$. At rank $r$ there are only $|I|r^2$ entries and finitely many such arrays. For indecomposable arrays $1\le r\le\lfloor D\rfloor$, so their union is finite. The empty category, if allowed, adds the single rank-zero array and is not indecomposable.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. For the canonical Frobenius algebra $(K,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\lambda)$ constructed in [[lem-canonical-fusion-category-algebra-is-frobenius]], set $t=\lambda\mu\Delta\eta$. Then $t\ne0$ and $s=t^{-1}\Delta$ is a $K$-bimodule section of multiplication. In particular $K$ is separable, and $e=s\eta$ satisfies
$$\mu e=\eta,\qquad(\mu\otimes\mathrm{id})(\mathrm{id}\otimes e)=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\mu)(e\otimes\mathrm{id}).$$

Let $A$ be an algebra object in a $k$-linear monoidal category and $B$ an $A$-bimodule. Suppose $e:\mathbf1\to A\otimes A$ satisfies
$$\mu e=\eta,\qquad (\mu\otimes\mathrm{id})(\mathrm{id}\otimes e)=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\mu)(e\otimes\mathrm{id}).$$
Set $C^n=\operatorname{Hom}(A^{\otimes n},B)$, with the Hochschild differential given by the alternating sum of the left action, adjacent multiplications, and the right action. Its normalized subcomplex consists of maps vanishing whenever any input is the unit $\eta$. For every $n\geq1$, define
$$h_n(f)=\lambda_B(\mathrm{id}_A\otimes f)(e\otimes\mathrm{id}_{A^{\otimes(n-1)}}),$$
where $\lambda_B$ denotes the left $A$-action. Then $h$ preserves the normalized subcomplex and $dh+hd=\mathrm{id}$ in every positive degree.

derivations.claim: Put $\mathcal E=\operatorname{Fun}_k(\mathcal M,\mathcal N)$ and $\mathcal Q=\operatorname{End}_k(\mathcal N)\boxtimes\operatorname{End}_k(\mathcal M)^{\mathrm{rev}}$. The action $(U\boxtimes V)\cdot S=USV$ makes $\mathcal E$ a $\mathcal Q$-module category. These underlying categories are finite semisimple: after choosing their finitely many simple objects, linear functors and transformations are finite matrices of vector spaces and linear maps. The two action functors give a tensor functor $\mathcal C\boxtimes\mathcal C^{\mathrm{rev}}\to\mathcal Q$. Let $A$ be the image of $K$ and $e_A$ the image of $e$; tensor functors preserve the two separability identities. The comparisons $\gamma$ give an action $\rho_T:A\cdot T\to T$: on a simple summand it is the adjoint of $\gamma_i:N_iT\to TM_i$, namely $N_iTM_{i^*}\to T$. The product and unit equations for this action are exactly the module-functor equations, as one sees by inserting $\sum q_a^rp_a^r=\mathrm{id}_{i\otimes j}$ in the displayed multiplication of $K$.

The object $B_T=\underline{\operatorname{End}}_{\mathcal Q}(T)$ represents $W\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal E}(W\cdot T,T)$: explicitly, sum each simple object of $\mathcal Q$ with the multiplicity of the corresponding finite-dimensional Hom space. Composition of evaluations makes $B_T$ an algebra, and $\rho_T$ corresponds to an algebra map $A\to B_T$. In particular $B_T$ is an $A$-bimodule. Internal-Hom adjunction and duality give isomorphisms $$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal Q}(A^{\otimes n},B_T)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal E}(A^{\otimes n}\cdot T,T)\cong C_T^n.$$ For the last map, the summand indexed by $(i_1,\ldots,i_n)$ is the adjunction $$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal E}(N_{i_1\otimes\cdots\otimes i_n}TM_{(i_1\otimes\cdots\otimes i_n)^*},T)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal E}(N_{i_1\otimes\cdots\otimes i_n}T,TM_{i_1\otimes\cdots\otimes i_n}).$$ The module associators identify tensor-word actions with the iterated actions in the statement. Values on simple tuples extend uniquely to natural transformations because every object is a finite direct sum of simples. Thus these maps are isomorphisms, not just injections into the cochain spaces.

Under these isomorphisms the two outer Hochschild faces compose with $\rho_T$ on the two sides; taking their adjoints gives precisely the zeroth and last cofaces displayed in the statement. For an interior face, the component $\sum_a p_a^r\boxtimes(q_a^r)^*$ of multiplication inserts $\sum_{r,a}q_a^rp_a^r=\mathrm{id}$ in the adjacent tensor factors; its adjoint is the merge coface, transported by the module associators. The unit of $A$ is the image of the unit summand of $K$, so the normalized conditions also agree. Consequently the maps in the preceding step identify the stated normalized complex with the normalized Hochschild complex of $A$ with coefficients $B_T$. This also proves $d^2=0$ for the stated differential.

Denote this complex isomorphism by $\Phi_n:C_T^n\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal Q}(A^{\otimes n},B_T)$. For $n\geq1$ define the required homotopy by $$h_n(f)=\Phi_{n-1}^{-1}\bigl(\lambda_{B_T}(\mathrm{id}_A\otimes\Phi_n(f))(e_A\otimes\mathrm{id}_{A^{\otimes(n-1)}})\bigr).$$ All maps in this formula have been specified in the preceding steps. Fact [F2] and the complex isomorphism give $d h_n+h_{n+1}d=\mathrm{id}_{C_T^n}$ and preservation of normalization. The same proof with $T=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal M}$ gives the action complex; replacing $\mathcal C$ by its tensor reversal gives the prescribed right-action convention. Thus every positive-degree cocycle is a coboundary, in particular every degree-two cocycle.

derivations.claim: Choose representatives $a$ of the finitely many simple objects of $\mathcal M$. Put $R(n)=\bigoplus_a\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal N}(F(a),n)\otimes_k a$ and $L(n)=\bigoplus_a\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal N}(n,F(a))^*\otimes_k a$. Since $\operatorname{End}(a)=k$, decomposition into these simples gives natural bijections $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal M}(m,Rn)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal N}(Fm,n)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal M}(Ln,m)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal N}(n,Fm)$. Define the units and counits to represent the identity maps under these bijections. The two triangle identities follow by applying either bijection: in each case the composite corresponds to the original identity. Thus these are actual ordinary adjunctions, with no exactness or representability assumption left implicit.

Let $(T,\mu,\eta,\sigma)$ be a separable monad on $\mathcal M$. Define $\mathcal M^T$ to consist of pairs $(x,a)$ with $a:Tx\to x$, $a\eta_x=1$ and $aT(a)=a\mu_x$; its arrows $h:(x,a)\to(y,b)$ obey $ha=bT(h)$. The underlying additive functor $T$ is exact because $\mathcal M$ is semisimple. Thus the kernel and cokernel of $h$ carry induced $T$-actions, by exactness and the universal properties, satisfying the two algebra equations. They give the categorical kernel and cokernel in $\mathcal M^T$. The canonical comparison from coimage to image is the underlying isomorphism and preserves actions; its inverse preserves them as well. Therefore $\mathcal M^T$ is abelian and the forgetful functor $U$ is exact and faithful. Its free left adjoint is $L_T(x)=(Tx,\mu_x)$, with unit $\eta_x$ and counit at $(x,a)$ equal to $a$. The two triangles are respectively $\mu_xT\eta_x=1$ and $a\eta_x=1$.

Fix a dual pair $X,X^\vee$ with evaluation $X\otimes X^\vee\to\mathbf1$ and coevaluation $\mathbf1\to X^\vee\otimes X$. Define $r_{n,X}:R(n\odot X)\to Rn\odot X$ by the following natural bijections in $m$: $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal M}(m,R(n\odot X))\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal N}(Fm,n\odot X)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal N}(F(m\odot X^\vee),n)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal M}(m\odot X^\vee,Rn)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal M}(m,Rn\odot X)$. The middle identification uses $f_{m,X^\vee}$ and the other identifications use the adjunction or the displayed duality. Every arrow is invertible, so Yoneda gives an invertible module comparison. To verify its pentagon, apply $\operatorname{Hom}(m,-)$ to the two paths for $X,Y$. Both paths move $Y^\vee$ and then $X^\vee$ across Hom, apply $f$ to the resulting action, then move them back. The equality of these composites is exactly the module pentagon for $f$, since evaluation of the dual of $X\otimes Y$ is the consecutive evaluation of $Y$ and $X$ with the associators. For $X=\mathbf1$ the same comparison reduces to the module unit equation for $f$. This proves all module-functor axioms for $R$.

For $(x,a)$ put $s_{(x,a)}=T(a)\sigma_x\eta_x:x\to Tx$. Its composite with $a$ is $aT(a)\sigma_x\eta_x=a\mu_x\sigma_x\eta_x=a\eta_x=1$. It is an algebra map to $(Tx,\mu_x)$: indeed $s a=T(a)\sigma_x\eta_xa=T(a)\sigma_xT(a)\eta_{Tx}=T(a)T^2(a)\sigma_{Tx}\eta_{Tx}=T(a)T(\mu_x)\sigma_{Tx}\eta_{Tx}=T(a)\sigma_x\mu_x\eta_{Tx}=T(a)\sigma_x$, while $\mu_xT(s)=\mu_xT^2(a)T(\sigma_x)T(\eta_x)=T(a)\mu_{Tx}T(\sigma_x)T(\eta_x)=T(a)\sigma_x\mu_xT(\eta_x)=T(a)\sigma_x$. Here the middle equalities use, in order, naturality, the algebra equation, the two bimodule equations for $\sigma$, and the unit equations. Naturality of $s$ in algebra maps follows by the same naturality of $\sigma,\eta$ and $ha=bT(h)$. Thus every algebra is a natural retract of its free algebra.

Under the bijections of step 2.1, the image of the adjunction counit $\epsilon_n:FRn\to n$ is its tensor translate, so the equality $(\epsilon_n\odot1_X)f_{Rn,X}F(r_{n,X})=\epsilon_{n\odot X}$ holds. This is precisely module-naturality of $\epsilon$. For the unit, apply the adjunction bijection to its two proposed module-naturality composites; both correspond to the identity of $F(m\odot X)$ after $f$ and its inverse cancel. Faithfulness of the bijection proves their equality. Hence both triangles from step 1.1 are identities of module-natural transformations. For $L$, use the dual pair with evaluation $X^\flat\otimes X\to\mathbf1$ and coevaluation $\mathbf1\to X\otimes X^\flat$ in the identical argument with the Hom adjunction reversed: $\operatorname{Hom}(L(n\odot X),m)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(n,Fm\odot X^\flat)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(Ln,m\odot X^\flat)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(Ln\odot X,m)$. Its middle comparison is that of $F$. Evaluation of tensor products gives the module pentagon, the unit pair gives its unit equation, and applying this bijection proves module-naturality of its unit and counit.

For each $x$, $L_T(x)$ is projective, since $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal M^T}(L_Tx,-)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal M}(x,U-)$ is exact. Hence all objects are projective by step 2.2. Let $g$ be the sum of the finitely many simples of $\mathcal M$. Every object of $\mathcal M^T$ is a quotient of a finite sum of copies of $L_Tg$: first its underlying object is a summand of a finite sum of copies of $g$, and then its action is an epimorphism from its free object. Also $\operatorname{End}(L_Tg)$ is finite dimensional, being a subspace of an underlying Hom space in $\mathcal M$. Every object has finite length, since a strict chain of subobjects remains a strict chain after the faithful exact functor $U$ and $U(x,a)=x$ has finite length. With all objects projective, all short exact sequences split, so each object is a finite sum of simples. Each simple is a summand of $L_Tg$ because its quotient from a finite sum of $L_Tg$ splits; the finite length of $L_Tg$ bounds the number of such simples. Thus $\mathcal M^T$ is finite semisimple with finite dimensional Hom spaces.

Write $t_{x,X}:T(x\odot X)\to Tx\odot X$ for the module comparison. Define $(x,a)\odot X=(x\odot X,(a\odot1)t_{x,X})$. The fact that $\mu$ and $\eta$ are module-natural proves its two algebra equations. The associativity and unit constraints inherited from $\mathcal M$ are algebra maps by the pentagon and unit equation for $t$, and obey their own pentagon and triangle because $U$ is faithful. Thus $\mathcal M^T$ is a finite semisimple right module category. The displayed action makes $U$ a module functor, and $t$ gives $L_T$ its module structure. Module-naturality of $\eta,\mu$ verifies the adjunction unit and counit. Module-naturality of $\sigma,\eta$ and of the action $a$ verifies that $s$ from step 2.2 is module-natural as well. Consequently $L_T\dashv U$ is a separable adjunction, induces exactly $T$ with its multiplication and unit, and supplies the required splitting.

In a monoidal category $\mathcal C$, an **algebra object** is an object $A$ with multiplication $m_A:A\otimes A\to A$ and unit $\eta_A:\mathbf1\to A$ satisfying associativity and unit equations with the associator and unitors of $\mathcal C$. It is **separable** if there is an $A$-bimodule morphism $\sigma_A:A\to A\otimes A$ with $m_A\sigma_A=1_A$. The composite $e_A=\sigma_A\eta_A:\mathbf1\to A\otimes A$ is its **separability element**. It satisfies $m_Ae_A=\eta_A$ and the centrality equation
$$ (m_A\otimes1_A)\circ(1_A\otimes e_A)=(1_A\otimes m_A)\circ(e_A\otimes1_A):A\longrightarrow A\otimes A,$$
with associators inserted. In element notation these are $\sum_i x_i y_i=1_A$ and $\sum_i a x_i\otimes y_i=\sum_i x_i\otimes y_i a$.

A **left $A$-module** is an object $M\in\mathcal C$ with an associative unital action $l_M:A\otimes M\to M$; a **right $A$-module** has an associative unital action $r_M:M\otimes A\to M$. Write $\operatorname{Mod}^{l}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ and $\operatorname{Mod}^{r}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ for their categories and module morphisms. The category of left $A$-modules is a right $\mathcal C$-module category by $M\odot X:=M\otimes X$, with left $A$-action obtained by associating $A\otimes(M\otimes X)$ to $(A\otimes M)\otimes X$ and applying $l_M\otimes1_X$, and the inherited associator and unitor. An **$A$-$B$ bimodule** is an object $X\in\mathcal C$ with commuting left and right actions $A\otimes X\to X$ and $X\otimes B\to X$, each associative and unital. A bimodule morphism preserves both actions.

The **regular $A$-$A$ bimodule** is the object $A$ with both actions given by $m_A$.

Given an $A$-$B$ bimodule $X$ and a $B$-$D$ bimodule $Y$, a morphism $q:X\otimes Y\to Z$ is **balanced over $B$** if
$$q\circ(r_X\otimes1_Y)=q\circ(1_X\otimes l_Y):X\otimes B\otimes Y\longrightarrow Z.$$
A relative tensor product $X\otimes_B Y$, when it exists, is an object with a balanced map $q_B:X\otimes Y\to X\otimes_B Y$ universal among balanced maps. Existence is not part of this definition.

An object of an abelian category is **semisimple** if it is a finite direct sum
of simple objects. The category is **semisimple** if every object is

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be algebraically closed of characteristic zero, let $G$ be a finite product of general linear groups, and let $X$ be a reduced affine variety of finite type with an algebraic $G$-action. If the differential of $f_x:G\to X$, $g\mapsto gx$, is surjective onto $T_xX$ at the identity for every $x\in X$, then every orbit is open and there are finitely many orbits. Empty products and the empty variety are allowed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The evaluation map is an isomorphism by semisimplicity and $\operatorname{End}(m_a)=k$; the latter follows since any element of a finite-dimensional division algebra over algebraically closed $k$ has an eigenvalue, so subtracting it gives a noninvertible element and hence zero. Fix one such array and fixed bases of $H_{ij}^k=\operatorname{Hom}(X_k,X_i\otimes X_j)$ in $\mathcal C$. Use its given associator and unitors as fixed matrices. The action is equivalently a strong tensor functor $F:\mathcal D\to\operatorname{End}_k(\mathcal V_r)$, where $\mathcal D=\mathcal C^{\mathrm{rev}}$ has $X\star Y=Y\otimes X$ and the target has tensor product composition. Naturality determines $J$ on all objects from these blocks: on direct sums it is blockwise this map, with the identity on external multiplicity spaces. Normalize $F_{\mathbf1}=\operatorname{id}$ and its unit comparison to the identity; then $J_{\mathbf1,X}$ and $J_{X,\mathbf1}$ are the fixed maps induced by the source unitors. This loses no structures: identify $F_{\mathbf1}$ with the identity by the given action unitor, transport all $J$ through that identification, and the module triangle forces the two stated values. Introduce the entries of every remaining simple-pair block $J$ and an additional scalar $t_J$ with equation $t_J\det J=1$. Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. For the canonical Frobenius algebra $(K,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\lambda)$ constructed in [[lem-canonical-fusion-category-algebra-is-frobenius]], set $t=\lambda\mu\Delta\eta$. Then $t\ne0$ and $s=t^{-1}\Delta$ is a $K$-bimodule section of multiplication. In particular $K$ is separable, and $e=s\eta$ satisfies
$$\mu e=\eta,\qquad(\mu\otimes\mathrm{id})(\mathrm{id}\otimes e)=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\mu)(e\otimes\mathrm{id}).$$

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over $k$. A **finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category** is a finite semisimple $k$-linear category $\mathcal M$ in the sense of [[def-semisimple-object-and-semisimple-abelian-category]], a bilinear action functor $\odot:\mathcal M\times\mathcal C\to\mathcal M$, and natural isomorphisms
$$\alpha_{m,X,Y}:(m\odot X)\odot Y\longrightarrow m\odot(X\otimes Y),\qquad \rho_m:m\odot\mathbf1\longrightarrow m,$$
which satisfy the module pentagon and triangle equations obtained from the associator and unitors of $\mathcal C$. The left-action convention is defined by reversing the order of the action factors.

A **module functor** $F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal N$ is a linear functor with natural action comparisons $F(m\odot X)\cong F(m)\odot X$ satisfying the module associativity and unit equations. A **module-natural transformation** is a natural transformation commuting with those comparisons. These objects, functors, and transformations form a 2-category denoted $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C)$ once its composition and monoidal product are specified.

This definition alone does not assert that there are finitely many equivalence classes of simple module categories, nor that $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C)$ is a fusion 2-category.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over an algebraically closed field $k$ and $\mathcal M$ a finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category. There is an algebra $A$ and a right module equivalence $\mathcal M\simeq\operatorname{Mod}^{l}_{\mathcal C}(A)$. This assertion does not yet assert separability. Fix the convention
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,[m,n])=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal M}(m\odot X,n).$$
One can take $A=[m,m]$ whenever $m$ is a module generator, meaning every object of $\mathcal M$ is a quotient of $m\odot X$ for some $X\in\mathcal C$. In particular the direct sum of the simple representatives is such a generator. The multiplication is specified below. For any such algebras $A,B$, a right exact right module functor from left $A$-modules to left $B$-modules is uniquely, up to canonical isomorphism, $P\mapsto Q\otimes_A P$ for a $B$-$A$ bimodule $Q$. The equivalence identifies module-natural transformations with bimodule maps. No braiding is assumed.

For a finite semisimple left $\mathcal C$-module category and a generator $m$ with every $n$ a quotient of $X\odot m$, the left-action version is $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,[m,n])=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal M}(X\odot m,n)$ and $n\mapsto[m,n]$ is an equivalence to right modules over $A=[m,m]$, with $[m,X\odot n]\cong X\otimes[m,n]$. This version likewise does not require or assert separability.

derivations.claim: The ordinary linear functor category $\mathcal E=\operatorname{Fun}_k(\mathcal M,\mathcal N)$ is finite semisimple: evaluation on representatives $m_a$ of the simples of $\mathcal M$, followed by decomposition in simples $n_b$ of $\mathcal N$, identifies it with the category of finite matrices of vector spaces $V_{ba}=\operatorname{Hom}(n_b,F(m_a))$. A natural transformation is exactly a matrix of linear maps; conversely the matrix defines the functor by additive extension. The category $\mathcal D$ acts on $\mathcal E$ by $(X\boxtimes Y)\cdot F=R_Y^{\mathcal N}FR_X^{\mathcal M}$. Indeed $R_YR_W=R_{W\otimes Y}$ and $R_ZR_X=R_{X\otimes Z}$, giving the product $(X\otimes Z)\boxtimes(W\otimes Y)$ in $\mathcal D$. The action coherence follows by applying the two module pentagons; its two unit equations are the two module triangles. Thus $K\cdot-$ is an exact linear monad on $\mathcal E$ with multiplication induced by that of $K$.

A left $K$-action on $F$ consists of components $\theta_{i,m}:F(m\odot i)\odot i^\vee\to F(m)$. By duality these correspond bijectively to $c_{m,i}:F(m\odot i)\to F(m)\odot i$; the inverse correspondence is $\theta_{i,m}=(1\odot\operatorname{ev}_i)(c_{m,i}\odot1)$. Finite semisimplicity extends these maps uniquely and naturally from simple $i$ to every $X$: decompose $X$ into simples, use additivity on the source, and the dual decomposition on the dual factor. Independence of bases follows from the identity $\sum_a g_a f_a=1_X$ for dual inclusion/projection maps. Expanding $\theta(\mu\cdot1)=\theta(1\cdot\theta)$ on the $(i,j)$ summand and using the formula for $\mu$ in F1 gives, after taking mates, $c_{m,i\otimes j}=(c_{m,i}\odot1_j)c_{m\odot i,j}$ with the module associators inserted: the sum over $f,g$ inserts exactly $\sum g f=1_{i\otimes j}$. The unit action equation gives $c_{m,\mathbf1}=1$ under the unitors. Conversely those two equations give the action equation on every summand of $K\otimes K$, hence on the full direct sum.

These initially lax comparisons are invertible by rigidity. Choose a dual $X^\flat$ with $b:\mathbf1\to X\otimes X^\flat$ and $d:X^\flat\otimes X\to\mathbf1$. An inverse to $c_{m,X}$ is the composite $F(m)\odot X\xrightarrow{F(1_m\odot b)\odot1_X}F(m\odot X\odot X^\flat)\odot X\xrightarrow{c_{m\odot X,X^\flat}\odot1_X}F(m\odot X)\odot X^\flat\odot X\xrightarrow{1\odot d}F(m\odot X)$. For its composite after $c_{m,X}$, naturality with $b$, followed by the product equation of step 2.1, leaves the zigzag $(1_X\otimes d)(b\otimes1_X)=1_X$. For the composite before $c_{m,X}$ use naturality with $d$ and the same product equation; the other zigzag and the unit equation leave $1_{F(m\odot X)}$. A map of $K$-actions is exactly a natural transformation commuting with all $\theta_i$, equivalently all $c_X$. Thus the category of $K$-modules in $\mathcal E$ is precisely $\operatorname{Fun}_{\mathcal C}(\mathcal M,\mathcal N)$, including its morphisms.

Kernels and cokernels of $K$-module maps exist and are their underlying kernels and cokernels in $\mathcal E$, since $K\cdot-$ is exact. They carry the induced actions by the universal properties. For modules $(P,\rho_P),(Q,\rho_Q)$ and an arbitrary underlying arrow $t:P\to Q$, put $\operatorname{Av}(t)=\rho_Q(1_K\cdot t)(1_K\cdot\rho_P)(e\cdot1_P)$. In symbolic notation for this composite it is $\operatorname{Av}(t)(p)=\sum_a x_a t(y_a p)$, where $e=\sum_a x_a\otimes y_a$ denotes the morphism $e$, not actual elements. Centrality says $\sum bx_a\otimes y_a=\sum x_a\otimes y_a b$, so associativity of the actions gives $\operatorname{Av}(t)(bp)=b\operatorname{Av}(t)(p)$ as an equality of the corresponding composites. Thus it is a module map. If $t$ already is a module map, the identity $\mu e=\eta$ gives $\operatorname{Av}(t)=t$. If $q:Q\to P$ is a module epimorphism and $qt=1_P$, the same formula gives $q\operatorname{Av}(t)=\operatorname{Av}(qt)=1_P$. Every underlying epi splits in $\mathcal E$, so all module epis split.

Hom spaces of modules are finite dimensional subspaces of those in $\mathcal E$. Every module has finite length, since its subobject chains give strict subobject chains in its underlying object of $\mathcal E$. Therefore the splitting in step 4.1 implies that every module is a finite direct sum of simples. To prove finiteness of the simple set, let $g$ be the sum of the finitely many simples of $\mathcal E$. The free module $K\cdot g$ has finite length. Every module is a quotient of a finite sum of copies of $K\cdot g$: its underlying object is a summand of a finite sum of copies of $g$, apply the free functor and then the action epimorphism. Each simple is therefore a summand of a finite sum of $K\cdot g$ and hence is isomorphic to a simple constituent of $K\cdot g$. There are only finitely many. Steps 3.1–5.1 prove the finite semisimplicity assertion. Under F2 this also proves it for the correctly oriented bimodule categories, without assuming separability of their representing algebras in advance.

A right module endofunctor $F$ of the regular category satisfies $F(X)=F(\mathbf1\otimes X)\cong F(\mathbf1)\otimes X$, naturally and compatibly with its comparison. Conversely $a\mapsto(a\otimes-)$ is a right module functor, with the associator as comparison. The same comparison shows that any module-natural transformation is $h\otimes1$ for its component $h$ at $\mathbf1$, and every $h$ defines one. Thus evaluation at $\mathbf1$ and $a\mapsto(a\otimes-)$ are inverse equivalences. The identity functor corresponds to $\mathbf1$, whose endomorphism algebra is $k$. Hence the identity 1-morphism of the regular module is simple, which is the asserted simple-unit condition.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over an algebraically closed field $k$, let $B$ be a separable algebra object, and let $X$ be an $A$-$B$ bimodule and $Y$ a $B$-$D$ bimodule. Put $e_B=\sigma_B\eta_B:\mathbf1\to B\otimes B$. The endomorphism
$$p_{X,Y}=(r_X\otimes l_Y)\circ(1_X\otimes e_B\otimes1_Y):X\otimes Y\to X\otimes Y$$
is idempotent. Its image, with the induced map $q_B:X\otimes Y\to\operatorname{im}(p_{X,Y})$, is the relative tensor product $X\otimes_B Y$: for every object $Z$, composition with $q_B$ gives a bijection from morphisms $\operatorname{im}(p_{X,Y})\to Z$ to maps $X\otimes Y\to Z$ balanced over $B$. The result is independent up to a unique canonical isomorphism of the chosen splitting of $p_{X,Y}$.

In a monoidal category $\mathcal C$, an **algebra object** is an object $A$ with multiplication $m_A:A\otimes A\to A$ and unit $\eta_A:\mathbf1\to A$ satisfying associativity and unit equations with the associator and unitors of $\mathcal C$. It is **separable** if there is an $A$-bimodule morphism $\sigma_A:A\to A\otimes A$ with $m_A\sigma_A=1_A$. The composite $e_A=\sigma_A\eta_A:\mathbf1\to A\otimes A$ is its **separability element**. It satisfies $m_Ae_A=\eta_A$ and the centrality equation
$$ (m_A\otimes1_A)\circ(1_A\otimes e_A)=(1_A\otimes m_A)\circ(e_A\otimes1_A):A\longrightarrow A\otimes A,$$
with associators inserted. In element notation these are $\sum_i x_i y_i=1_A$ and $\sum_i a x_i\otimes y_i=\sum_i x_i\otimes y_i a$.

A **left $A$-module** is an object $M\in\mathcal C$ with an associative unital action $l_M:A\otimes M\to M$; a **right $A$-module** has an associative unital action $r_M:M\otimes A\to M$. Write $\operatorname{Mod}^{l}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ and $\operatorname{Mod}^{r}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ for their categories and module morphisms. The category of left $A$-modules is a right $\mathcal C$-module category by $M\odot X:=M\otimes X$, with left $A$-action obtained by associating $A\otimes(M\otimes X)$ to $(A\otimes M)\otimes X$ and applying $l_M\otimes1_X$, and the inherited associator and unitor. An **$A$-$B$ bimodule** is an object $X\in\mathcal C$ with commuting left and right actions $A\otimes X\to X$ and $X\otimes B\to X$, each associative and unital. A bimodule morphism preserves both actions.

The **regular $A$-$A$ bimodule** is the object $A$ with both actions given by $m_A$.

Given an $A$-$B$ bimodule $X$ and a $B$-$D$ bimodule $Y$, a morphism $q:X\otimes Y\to Z$ is **balanced over $B$** if
$$q\circ(r_X\otimes1_Y)=q\circ(1_X\otimes l_Y):X\otimes B\otimes Y\longrightarrow Z.$$
A relative tensor product $X\otimes_B Y$, when it exists, is an object with a balanced map $q_B:X\otimes Y\to X\otimes_B Y$ universal among balanced maps. Existence is not part of this definition.

derivations.claim: Let $X:A\to B$, $Y:B\to D$, and $Z:D\to E$. Both $(X\otimes_B Y)\otimes_D Z$ and $X\otimes_B(Y\otimes_D Z)$ receive a map from $X\otimes Y\otimes Z$ that is balanced in the $B$- and $D$-slots. Conversely, a map from $X\otimes Y\otimes Z$ balanced in both slots factors uniquely through either parenthesization: first apply the universal property in [F1] to one slot, then to the other. The two iterated products therefore represent the same functor of the target object.

The representing property in step 1.1 gives a unique isomorphism $a_{X,Y,Z}:(X\otimes_B Y)\otimes_D Z\longrightarrow X\otimes_B(Y\otimes_D Z)$ preserving the universal three-balanced map; applying the same property in reverse gives its inverse. For four composable bimodules, both composites around the pentagon preserve the same universal four-balanced map. Uniqueness therefore makes the two composites equal, which is the pentagon equation.

The regular bimodule $A$ is a left and right unit. The action maps $A\otimes_A X\to X$ and $X\otimes_A A\to X$ are balanced. Their inverses are induced by the algebra unit $\eta_A$ and the relevant unitors. The action and unit laws show the two composites are identities; the triangle equation for these unitors follows because its two paths agree on the universal balanced map, so step 1.1 forces equality.

Bimodule maps $f:X\to X'$ and $g:Y\to Y'$ induce the unique map $f\otimes_B g$ preserving the universal balanced map. For composable triples of bimodule maps, either horizontal-then-vertical or vertical-then-horizontal composition has the same composite with that universal map, since each is the ordinary composite of $f,g$ on the tensor factors. Uniqueness from [F1] gives equality; this is interchange. Thus these data form the stated bicategory.

Define the monoidal opposite $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{mp}}$ to have the same objects and morphisms, tensor product $X\otimes_{\mathrm{mp}}Y:=Y\otimes X$, associator $\alpha^{\mathrm{mp}}_{X,Y,Z}:=\alpha^{-1}_{Z,Y,X}$, and unitors $\lambda^{\mathrm{mp}}_X:=\rho_X$, $\rho^{\mathrm{mp}}_X:=\lambda_X$. The braiding defines a strong monoidal equivalence $J:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{mp}}\to\mathcal C$ that is the identity on the underlying category and has tensorator $c_{Y,X}^{-1}:X\otimes Y\to Y\otimes X$.

Regard $A$ as an algebra in $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{mp}}$ with the same unit and multiplication $m:A\otimes_{\mathrm{mp}}A=A\otimes A\to A$. Its transport along $J$ is the **opposite algebra** $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ in $\mathcal C$; its multiplication is
$$m_{A^{\mathrm{op}}}=m\circ c_{A,A}^{-1}:A\otimes A\to A,$$
and its unit is $\eta$. This convention fixes the braiding direction. The hexagon identities are the tensorator coherence of $J$, and its unit coherence follows from the braiding unit equations.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided fusion category and let $A,B$ be separable algebra objects, with bimodule sections $\sigma_A,\sigma_B$. Give $A\otimes B$ the braided tensor-product algebra structure from [[thm-braided-category-tensor-product-algebra-structure]]. A separability section is
$$\sigma_{A\otimes B}=(1_A\otimes c_{B,A}^{-1}\otimes1_B)\circ(\sigma_A\otimes\sigma_B):A\otimes B\longrightarrow(A\otimes B)\otimes(A\otimes B).$$
This is an $A\otimes B$-bimodule map and its composite with multiplication is the identity.

For separable algebra objects in a finite semisimple monoidal category, take objects to be separable algebras, 1-morphisms $A\to B$ to be $A$-$B$ bimodules, and 2-morphisms to be bimodule maps. Composition is $X\circ Y=X\otimes_B Y$ with order fixed so $X:A\to B$ and $Y:B\to D$ compose as $X\otimes_B Y:A\to D$. This composition has canonical associators and unitors satisfying the bicategory pentagon and interchange equations; its units are the regular bimodules $_AA_A$.

In a monoidal category $\mathcal C$, an **algebra object** is an object $A$ with multiplication $m_A:A\otimes A\to A$ and unit $\eta_A:\mathbf1\to A$ satisfying associativity and unit equations with the associator and unitors of $\mathcal C$. It is **separable** if there is an $A$-bimodule morphism $\sigma_A:A\to A\otimes A$ with $m_A\sigma_A=1_A$. The composite $e_A=\sigma_A\eta_A:\mathbf1\to A\otimes A$ is its **separability element**. It satisfies $m_Ae_A=\eta_A$ and the centrality equation
$$ (m_A\otimes1_A)\circ(1_A\otimes e_A)=(1_A\otimes m_A)\circ(e_A\otimes1_A):A\longrightarrow A\otimes A,$$
with associators inserted. In element notation these are $\sum_i x_i y_i=1_A$ and $\sum_i a x_i\otimes y_i=\sum_i x_i\otimes y_i a$.

A **left $A$-module** is an object $M\in\mathcal C$ with an associative unital action $l_M:A\otimes M\to M$; a **right $A$-module** has an associative unital action $r_M:M\otimes A\to M$. Write $\operatorname{Mod}^{l}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ and $\operatorname{Mod}^{r}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ for their categories and module morphisms. The category of left $A$-modules is a right $\mathcal C$-module category by $M\odot X:=M\otimes X$, with left $A$-action obtained by associating $A\otimes(M\otimes X)$ to $(A\otimes M)\otimes X$ and applying $l_M\otimes1_X$, and the inherited associator and unitor. An **$A$-$B$ bimodule** is an object $X\in\mathcal C$ with commuting left and right actions $A\otimes X\to X$ and $X\otimes B\to X$, each associative and unital. A bimodule morphism preserves both actions.

The **regular $A$-$A$ bimodule** is the object $A$ with both actions given by $m_A$.

Given an $A$-$B$ bimodule $X$ and a $B$-$D$ bimodule $Y$, a morphism $q:X\otimes Y\to Z$ is **balanced over $B$** if
$$q\circ(r_X\otimes1_Y)=q\circ(1_X\otimes l_Y):X\otimes B\otimes Y\longrightarrow Z.$$
A relative tensor product $X\otimes_B Y$, when it exists, is an object with a balanced map $q_B:X\otimes Y\to X\otimes_B Y$ universal among balanced maps. Existence is not part of this definition.

Let $G$ be a finite group ([[def-group]]), with identity $e$. A normalized multiplicative 4-cochain is a function $\omega:G^4\to k^\times$ equal to $1$ whenever any argument is $e$. It is a **group 4-cocycle** when, for all $g,h,k,l,m\in G$,
$$\omega(h,k,l,m)\omega(g,hk,l,m)\omega(g,h,k,lm)=\omega(gh,k,l,m)\omega(g,h,kl,m)\omega(g,h,k,l).$$

On $2\mathrm{Vect}_G$, define the tensor product by convolution:
$$\left(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B\right)_u=\bigoplus_{gh=u}\mathcal A_g\boxtimes\mathcal B_h,$$
where $\boxtimes$ is the finite semisimple tensor product of linear categories. The unit is $\mathrm{Vect}_k$ concentrated in degree $e$. The associator and unitors are the canonical rebracketing and unit equivalences. On four homogeneous inputs of degrees $g,h,k,l$, prescribe the pentagonator to be multiplication by the scalar $\omega(g,h,k,l)$ on every simple summand; extend it by direct sums and naturality. Denote this proposed weak monoidal 2-category structure by $2\mathrm{Vect}^{\omega}_G$.

The scalar is central, so its naturality is componentwise. The displayed group equation is the exact coherence condition to be checked for five homogeneous inputs. This definition includes no braiding and no claim about classification of all fusion 2-categories.

Fix an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic zero and a finite group $G$ ([[def-group]]). A finite semisimple category is understood in the sense of [[def-semisimple-object-and-semisimple-abelian-category]], with simple objects as in [[def-simple-object]]. A **finite semisimple $G$-graded $k$-linear category** is a finite semisimple $k$-linear category $\mathcal A$ together with a direct-sum decomposition
$$\mathcal A=\bigoplus_{g\in G}\mathcal A_g.$$
An object in $\mathcal A_g$ is homogeneous of degree $g$. A grading-preserving linear functor sends each $\mathcal A_g$ into the corresponding degree-$g$ summand, and its 2-morphisms are natural transformations. Such categories, functors, and natural transformations form the underlying 2-category denoted $2\mathrm{Vect}_G$.

For finite semisimple categories $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ with simple-label sets $S,T$, their finite semisimple tensor product $\mathcal A\boxtimes\mathcal B$ has simple labels $S\times T$ and
$$\operatorname{Hom}(s\boxtimes t,s'\boxtimes t')=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(s,s')\otimes_k\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal B}(t,t'),$$
extended to direct sums. For a concrete skeleton, choose finite sets $S_g$ of simple labels and replace $\mathcal A_g$ by the category of finite-dimensional $k$-vector-space families indexed by $S_g$. A linear functor is represented by a finite matrix of finite-dimensional vector spaces within each grade. This skeleton fixes the meaning of “finite” and the homogeneous components; it does not assert any physical realization.

A **fusion 2-category** is a finite semisimple linear 2-category with a weak monoidal structure, a simple monoidal unit, and left and right duals for every object. For a right dual $A^\#$ of $A$, the duality data include 1-morphisms
$$e_A:A\otimes A^\#\to I,\qquad i_A:I\to A^\#\otimes A,$$
and invertible cusp 2-morphisms from $(e_A\otimes A)\circ(A\otimes i_A)$ to $1_A$ and from $(A^\#\otimes e_A)\circ(i_A\otimes A^\#)$ to $1_{A^\#}$, with the associator and unitors inserted at the indicated sources and targets.

Here “simple unit” means that $1_I$ is a simple 1-morphism. A pivotal or spherical enhancement is extra structure: it requires its own duality coherence and trace axioms. Neither such enhancement nor a spherical trace is included in “fusion 2-category.”

A **group** is a monoid $(G,*,e)$ ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]) in which every
element is invertible ([[def-invertible-element]]). Written out, a group is a set
$G$ with a binary operation $*$ ([[def-binary-operation]]) and an element
$e \in G$ such that

- **(G1)** $(x * y) * z = x * (y * z)$ for all $x, y, z \in G$;
- **(G2)** $e * x = x = x * e$ for every $x \in G$;
- **(G3)** for every $x \in G$ there is $y \in G$ with $y * x = e = x * y$.

By [[lem-identity-unique]] the element $e$ of (G2) is unique, and by
[[lem-inverse-unique]] the element $y$ of (G3) is unique for each $x$ and is
determined by either one of the two equations alone. So the notations $e$ for the
identity and $x^{-1}$ for the inverse of $x$ are legitimate, and asserting
$y * x = e$ alone already says $y = x^{-1}$.

A group is **abelian**, or **commutative**, when its operation is commutative:
$x * y = y * x$ for all $x, y \in G$.

**Notation.** The operation is usually written multiplicatively, $xy$ for
$x * y$, with identity $e$ (or $1$) and inverse $x^{-1}$. For an abelian group it
is often written additively, $x + y$, with identity $0$ and inverse $-x$; the two
notations describe the same notion and nothing below depends on the choice. We
write $G$ for the group when the operation is understood.

derivations.claim: For homogeneous inputs of grades $g,h,k,l,m$, the two composites of pentagonators have scalar coefficients $\omega(h,k,l,m)\omega(g,hk,l,m)\omega(g,h,k,lm)\quad\hbox{and}\quad\omega(gh,k,l,m)\omega(g,h,kl,m)\omega(g,h,k,l).$ They agree by the 4-cocycle equation in [F1]. On arbitrary objects both pastings are direct sums of these homogeneous components, and their naturality makes the componentwise equality an equality of modifications. Every coherence equation with a unit input reduces to the identity scalar by normalization in [F1].

Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ have respectively $n_g,m_g$ simple labels in grade $g$. A grading-preserving linear functor $\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ is a family of matrices of finite-dimensional vector spaces, one $m_g$-by-$n_g$ matrix for each $g$. Consequently its hom category is a finite product of finite matrix categories over $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb C}$. Each matrix category is semisimple: its simple objects have one copy of $\mathbb C$ in a single matrix entry and zero elsewhere, and every matrix is a finite direct sum of these. Composition is matrix multiplication with direct sums and tensor products of finite-dimensional vector spaces. Object direct sums are concatenation of the finite simple-label sets. This proves the hom-category and direct-sum clauses of [F3].

If $F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ is represented by matrices $V_{ji}$, define its right adjoint by the transposed matrices $(F^R)_{ij}=V_{ji}^*$, where $V^*$ is the ordinary finite-dimensional vector-space dual; define its left adjoint using the opposite duality. The unit and counit are the direct sums of the vector-space coevaluation and evaluation maps. Each triangle composite is the identity on every matrix entry by the vector-space dual-basis identities, so these are left and right adjoints.

Let $S=\bigsqcup_{g\in G}S_g$ be the finite simple-label set of $\mathcal A\simeq\mathrm{Vec}^{S}$. A grading-preserving monad $T$ has finite matrix entries $T_{t,s}$, zero unless $s,t$ have the same grade. Its unit and multiplication satisfy the monad unit and associativity laws; these are exactly the identity and composition laws for the finite $k$-linear category with objects $S$ and morphism spaces $T_{t,s}$. Its finite-dimensional category algebra $R_T=\bigoplus_{s,t\in S}T_{t,s}$ has unit the sum of the object identities, and a $T$-algebra is exactly a family $(M_s)_{s\in S}$ with compatible left $R_T$-action maps $T_{t,s}\otimes M_s\to M_t$. The separability section $\sigma:T\Rightarrow T^2$ gives $E=\sigma\eta(1)=\sum_i x_i\otimes y_i\in R_T\otimes R_T$; the equations $\mu\sigma=1_T$ and $T$-bilinearity of $\sigma$ say respectively $\sum_i x_i y_i=1_{R_T}$ and $aE=Ea$ for every $a\in R_T$, component by component. For a surjective homomorphism $p:M\to N$ of finite-dimensional left $R_T$-modules, choose a $k$-linear section $s$ and set $\bar s(n)=\sum_i x_i\,s(y_i n)$. Then $p\bar s(n)=\sum_i x_i y_i n=n$, while $\bar s(a n)=\sum_i x_i s(y_i a n)=\sum_i (a x_i)s(y_i n)=a\bar s(n)$ by $Ea=aE$. Thus every module epimorphism splits; every finite-dimensional module is a quotient of a finite direct sum of copies of the regular module, by choosing a finite vector-space generating set, so it is projective and the finite-dimensional module category is semisimple. Every simple module is a quotient of the regular module, which has finite length, so there are finitely many simple classes. Since $R_T$ has no entries between different grades, its central grade idempotents split this Eilenberg–Moore category into finitely many finite semisimple grade pieces. The free functor $F$ sends $X$ to $(TX,\mu_X)$ and is left adjoint to the forgetful functor $U$: the adjunction bijection sends an algebra map $f:TX\to M$ to $f\eta_X$, with inverse $g\mapsto a_M\circ T(g)$ for a $T$-algebra action $a_M$. The monad and algebra laws verify that these maps are inverse. Both functors preserve grades, and $UF=T$ with unit $\eta$ and multiplication $\mu$. Hence the Eilenberg–Moore category and the adjunction $F\dashv U$ give the required separable-monad splitting in $2\mathrm{Vect}^{\omega}_G$.

Tensoring linear functors on separate factors has the canonical comparison that sends an elementary tensor $x\otimes y$ to $F(x)\otimes G(y)$. The two sides of each interchange equation therefore agree on elementary tensors and hence on the entire tensor product. The scalar in [F1] commutes with every linear map, so the pentagonator is natural in 1- and 2-morphisms. Thus the prescribed operations satisfy the pseudofunctor and naturality parts of the weak monoidal 2-category definition.

The identity functor of a finite semisimple category with simple labels $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ is the direct sum of the $n$ projection-inclusion functors for those labels. Each summand is simple, so the identity is simple exactly when $n=1$. The only simple objects of $2\mathrm{Vect}^{\omega}_G$ are therefore the one-label categories $\delta_g$, one for each $g\in G$. In particular $\delta_e$ is the unique simple summand of the monoidal unit and is simple.

For an object with simple labels $s_{g,i}$, put the dual label $s_{g,i}^{\#}$ in grade $g^{-1}$. Evaluation sends $(s_{g,i},s_{h,j}^{\#})$ to $\mathbb C$ when $h=g$ and $j=i$, and to $0$ otherwise; coevaluation sends $\mathbb C$ to the direct sum of $s_{g,i}^{\#}\otimes s_{g,i}$ over all labels. Each right-dual triangle composite is the identity on every simple label, since only its matching diagonal summand survives; reversing evaluation and coevaluation gives the same check for left duals. Thus both cusp transformations have scalar $1$. These composites use only the associator and unitors on at most three object factors; the 4-cocycle enters the four-input pentagonator already checked in step 1.1, and normalized unit cases contribute scalar $1$. This supplies duals without asserting a pivotal or spherical enhancement.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided fusion category and let $\mathcal M,\mathcal N$ be finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module categories. A **relative Deligne product** $\mathcal M\boxtimes_{\mathcal C}\mathcal N$ in $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C)$ means a finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category $\mathcal P$ equipped with an exact bilinear functor $b:\mathcal M\times\mathcal N\to\mathcal P$ that is balanced over the middle $\mathcal C$-action and compatible with the outer right $\mathcal C$-action, and is universal among such functors: for every finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category $\mathcal D$, composition with $b$ gives an equivalence between right $\mathcal C$-module functors $\mathcal P\to\mathcal D$ and exact bilinear middle-balanced right $\mathcal C$-module functors $\mathcal M\times\mathcal N\to\mathcal D$.

For the balancing convention, a right module category $\mathcal N$ is regarded as a left module category by $X\triangleright n:=n\odot X$. Its left module associator $(X\otimes Y)\triangleright n\to X\triangleright(Y\triangleright n)$ is the composite of $n\odot c_{Y,X}^{-1}$ with the inverse right-module associator. “Balanced” means that $b(m\odot X,n)\cong b(m,X\triangleright n)$ naturally in all variables, compatibly with the unit and associativity constraints. This definition fixes the universal property and the braiding convention; it does not assert that a product exists.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided fusion category and let $A,B$ be separable algebra objects, with bimodule sections $\sigma_A,\sigma_B$. Give $A\otimes B$ the braided tensor-product algebra structure from [[thm-braided-category-tensor-product-algebra-structure]]. A separability section is
$$\sigma_{A\otimes B}=(1_A\otimes c_{B,A}^{-1}\otimes1_B)\circ(\sigma_A\otimes\sigma_B):A\otimes B\longrightarrow(A\otimes B)\otimes(A\otimes B).$$
This is an $A\otimes B$-bimodule map and its composite with multiplication is the identity.

Let $A,B$ be separable algebra objects in a fusion category $\mathcal C$. The categories of left $A$-modules, right $B$-modules and $A$-$B$ bimodules are finite semisimple. This assertion is valid in any characteristic in which the stated separability sections exist. In particular the left $A$-modules, with action $P\odot X=P\otimes X$, form a finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category.

In a monoidal category $\mathcal C$, an **algebra object** is an object $A$ with multiplication $m_A:A\otimes A\to A$ and unit $\eta_A:\mathbf1\to A$ satisfying associativity and unit equations with the associator and unitors of $\mathcal C$. It is **separable** if there is an $A$-bimodule morphism $\sigma_A:A\to A\otimes A$ with $m_A\sigma_A=1_A$. The composite $e_A=\sigma_A\eta_A:\mathbf1\to A\otimes A$ is its **separability element**. It satisfies $m_Ae_A=\eta_A$ and the centrality equation
$$ (m_A\otimes1_A)\circ(1_A\otimes e_A)=(1_A\otimes m_A)\circ(e_A\otimes1_A):A\longrightarrow A\otimes A,$$
with associators inserted. In element notation these are $\sum_i x_i y_i=1_A$ and $\sum_i a x_i\otimes y_i=\sum_i x_i\otimes y_i a$.

A **left $A$-module** is an object $M\in\mathcal C$ with an associative unital action $l_M:A\otimes M\to M$; a **right $A$-module** has an associative unital action $r_M:M\otimes A\to M$. Write $\operatorname{Mod}^{l}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ and $\operatorname{Mod}^{r}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ for their categories and module morphisms. The category of left $A$-modules is a right $\mathcal C$-module category by $M\odot X:=M\otimes X$, with left $A$-action obtained by associating $A\otimes(M\otimes X)$ to $(A\otimes M)\otimes X$ and applying $l_M\otimes1_X$, and the inherited associator and unitor. An **$A$-$B$ bimodule** is an object $X\in\mathcal C$ with commuting left and right actions $A\otimes X\to X$ and $X\otimes B\to X$, each associative and unital. A bimodule morphism preserves both actions.

The **regular $A$-$A$ bimodule** is the object $A$ with both actions given by $m_A$.

Given an $A$-$B$ bimodule $X$ and a $B$-$D$ bimodule $Y$, a morphism $q:X\otimes Y\to Z$ is **balanced over $B$** if
$$q\circ(r_X\otimes1_Y)=q\circ(1_X\otimes l_Y):X\otimes B\otimes Y\longrightarrow Z.$$
A relative tensor product $X\otimes_B Y$, when it exists, is an object with a balanced map $q_B:X\otimes Y\to X\otimes_B Y$ universal among balanced maps. Existence is not part of this definition.

derivations.claim: The left-module presentation reverses the algebra-bimodule $1$-morphism orientation: a module functor $\operatorname{Mod}^l(A)\to\operatorname{Mod}^l(B)$ is represented by a $B$-$A$ bimodule, while the algebra convention $A\to B$ uses $A$-$B$ bimodules. Thus the algebra presentation of this module $2$-category uses the $1$-morphism opposite of that algebra bicategory. Tensor multiplication on objects is unchanged. Under this passage the evaluation and coevaluation arrows exchange, and left and right dual roles exchange; both dual orientations have been constructed separately. Preserve the positive braided tensor algebra K=A⊗B. Let P=Mod^l_C(K). Define b(M,N)=M⊗N, with K-action `(l_M⊗l_N)(1_A⊗c_{B,M}⊗1_N)`.

Naturality and the hexagons prove its action equation exactly as for the positive tensor-algebra multiplication. Define balance by `1_M⊗c_{N,X}^{-1}: MXN→MNX`; this is K-linear: expand c_{B,MX}, cancel the c_{B,X} against c_{N,X}^{-1} by naturality with l_N, and the remaining composite is the target K-action. The balance/unit equation is the braiding unit equation. For balance associativity on $MXYN$, both composites are the inverse braid taking $XYN$ to $NYX$: move $Y$ behind $N$ and then $X$ behind $NY$, or move $XY$ behind $N$ and then interchange $X,Y$ by $c_{Y,X}^{-1}$. The inverse hexagon expands both to the same three inverse crossings. Compatibility with the outer right action is the other inverse hexagon. Hence b is a balanced right-module functor. It is exact and bilinear because all tensor functors in a fusion category are exact.

Here is a proof of universality which also specifies its action on transformations. A right K-object d in a finite semisimple right C-module category D is an object equipped with r:d⊙K→d satisfying the algebra action equations. It determines a module functor H_d:P→D by `H_d(L)=d⊙_K L`,

constructed as the image of the separability idempotent `(r⊙l_L)(1_d⊙e_K⊙1_L)` on d⊙L. Its image exists because D is finite semisimple. The usual centrality and unit equations for e_K show this image corepresents K-balanced maps, just as for the ordinary bimodule supplier: the idempotent is fixed by every balanced map; conversely its projection is balanced. No new coequalizer existence theorem is being assumed. This construction is functorial in L and K-linear maps d→d'.

Conversely any module functor H:P→D is canonically H_d with d=H(K). Its right action is H(m_K):H(K⊗K)≅H(K)⊙K→H(K). On free modules K⊗X, its module constraint gives H(K⊗X)≅d⊙X. Every K-module L is a retract of K⊗L: the action is the retraction and the section is `(1_K⊗l_L)(e_K⊗1_L)`. This section is K-linear by centrality, and its action composite is 1_L. Hence the free-module comparison extends uniquely to all retracts. To check naturality it suffices to check free maps. Such a map K⊗X→K⊗Y is uniquely `(m_K⊗1_Y)(1_K⊗f)` for f:X→K⊗Y obtained by inserting η_K; H and H_d agree on this expression by the definition of r. Transformations agree precisely when their value at K is K-linear. This proves an equivalence of categories, including transformations, between module functors P→D and right K-objects in D. For a balanced module functor F:Mod^l(A)×Mod^l(B)→D, put d=F(A,B). Denote its outer constraint by `δ:F(M,NX)→F(M,N)⊙X` and its balance by β. Put `θ=δβ:F(MX,N)→F(M,N)⊙X`. Define `r_A=F(m_A,1_B) θ_{A,A,B}^{-1}:d⊙A→d`, `r_B=F(1_A,m_B) δ_{A,B,B}^{-1}:d⊙B→d`.

Naturality with the algebra multiplications proves their associative/unital action equations. Expanding the balance/outer compatibility square gives the precise exchange equation `r_A(r_B⊙1_A)=r_B(r_A⊙1_B)(1_d⊙c_{B,A}):d⊙B⊙A→d`.

For an explicit verification, replace θ by δβ, move each multiplication through δ by its naturality, and through β by naturality in its module arguments. The residual two routes move the free B slot past the free A slot. The balance-associativity equation for the chosen inverse left conversion replaces that move by c_{B,A}; its inverse crossing is cancelled by the inverse in θ^-1. The remaining maps are F(m_A,m_B) on both routes. Thus `r=r_B(r_A⊙1_B)` is a right K-action: its iterated action on dABAB first moves the middle B past A by c_{B,A}, then uses the two individual action equations, exactly giving r(1_d⊙m_K). This proves the action equation without assuming ordinary commuting actions.

The functor H_d b is canonically equivalent to F. On free pairs first use δ to identify $F(AX,BY)$ with $F(AX,B)\odot Y$, and then θ on the first factor, to obtain `F(A⊗X,B⊗Y)≅d⊙X⊙Y`. Meanwhile the positive crossing `1_A⊗c_{B,X}⊗1_Y` is a K-linear isomorphism `K⊗X⊗Y→b(A⊗X,B⊗Y)`;

it identifies H_d b on this pair with d⊙X⊙Y. The two identifications commute with arbitrary free A-module and B-module morphisms: express such morphisms by their adjoint maps X→A⊗X' and Y→B⊗Y', then use r_A,r_B respectively. For a simultaneous morphism the exchange equation is exactly the required compatibility of the two orders. Every M,N is a retract of its free module by the displayed separability section, so this natural equivalence extends to all pairs by taking images of the two commuting retract idempotents. The construction respects the balance and outer action because it does so on free pairs, where these equations are the already verified β,δ equations. Thus composition with b is essentially surjective on balanced functors.

A transformation between two balanced functors is determined on free pairs by its component at (A,B), using θ,δ, and then on all pairs by retracts. Naturality with m_A and m_B says exactly that this component preserves r_A,r_B, equivalently the K-action r. Conversely any K-linear component gives such a transformation via H_d. Consequently composition with b is fully faithful and is the required equivalence of categories. This proves the exact stated universal property, not merely existence of a bilinear functor.

Finite semisimplicity of P follows from separability of K: module Hom spaces are images of the averaging idempotent on Hom_C(M,N), so are finite dimensional; every module is a retract of a free module, and the finitely many free modules K⊗S_i for simple S_i of C form a finite additive generator. Its endomorphism algebra is semisimple because any module subobject splits by averaging an underlying splitting. Therefore the module category is finite semisimple. It is a right C-module category by the inherited tensor action. The preceding argument applies to arbitrary D, so uniqueness of representing objects makes the answer independent of the chosen algebra presentations, with a canonical equivalence preserving b.

For module functors G:M→M',H:N→N', apply the universal property to b'(G×H); its balanced structure is inherited from the module constraints of G,H. This defines G⊠H. For module-natural transformations use full faithfulness to define their product. Identity and composite comparison maps are the unique maps whose pullbacks to b equal the identity or the corresponding composite constraint. Their associativity, unit and interchange equations hold by full faithfulness, since after pullback they are the same equation for ordinary functor composition.

Both parenthesizations of three module categories represent the category of three-variable exact functors balanced in the two adjacent slots, with outer right-module compatibility. This follows by applying the just-proved equivalence twice; the same free/retract argument shows that no balanced transformations are lost. Their comparison is therefore the unique equivalence preserving the universal three-variable functor, with its specified natural isomorphism. For the regular module category C, the action functor M×C→M (and the converted left action C×M→M) has the universal property by inserting the unit object and applying balance. These give the unitors. On four variables the two pentagon composites have the same pullback comparison to the universal four-variable functor. Full faithfulness gives the unique pentagonator modification; on five variables the two composites of these modifications have identical pullback, hence are equal. The unitor triangle modification and all its compatibility equations follow in exactly the same way from the three-variable functor with a unit slot. This is the weak monoidal 2-category coherence assertion: one should say 'canonical modifications' rather than incorrectly demanding literal equality of unchosen equivalences. Naturality with G,H and their transformations follows by pulling back to the same multivariable functor. Thus the product supplies all morphism levels and weak coherence required in the carrier statement.

Let $G$ be a finite group ([[def-group]]), with identity $e$. A normalized multiplicative 4-cochain is a function $\omega:G^4\to k^\times$ equal to $1$ whenever any argument is $e$. It is a **group 4-cocycle** when, for all $g,h,k,l,m\in G$,
$$\omega(h,k,l,m)\omega(g,hk,l,m)\omega(g,h,k,lm)=\omega(gh,k,l,m)\omega(g,h,kl,m)\omega(g,h,k,l).$$

On $2\mathrm{Vect}_G$, define the tensor product by convolution:
$$\left(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B\right)_u=\bigoplus_{gh=u}\mathcal A_g\boxtimes\mathcal B_h,$$
where $\boxtimes$ is the finite semisimple tensor product of linear categories. The unit is $\mathrm{Vect}_k$ concentrated in degree $e$. The associator and unitors are the canonical rebracketing and unit equivalences. On four homogeneous inputs of degrees $g,h,k,l$, prescribe the pentagonator to be multiplication by the scalar $\omega(g,h,k,l)$ on every simple summand; extend it by direct sums and naturality. Denote this proposed weak monoidal 2-category structure by $2\mathrm{Vect}^{\omega}_G$.

The scalar is central, so its naturality is componentwise. The displayed group equation is the exact coherence condition to be checked for five homogeneous inputs. This definition includes no braiding and no claim about classification of all fusion 2-categories.

derivations.claim: The multiplicative coboundary on a normalized 3-cochain is the five-factor expression in the statement. Its coboundary is $1$: writing $\delta=\prod_i d_i^{(-1)^i}$, where $d_0$ drops the first group element, $d_4$ drops the last, and each interior $d_i$ multiplies adjacent entries, the identities $d_jd_i=d_id_{j-1}$ for $i<j$ pair every factor of $\delta^2\beta$ with its inverse. The interior identities are exactly associativity in $G$. Hence $\omega\delta\beta$ is a 4-cocycle whenever $\omega$ is. Normalization of $\beta$ makes $\delta\beta$ equal to $1$ if any input is $e$.

Define the underlying pseudofunctor to be the identity on objects, functors, and natural transformations; take its tensorator and unitator to be identity equivalences. For each triple of homogeneous input degrees $(g,h,k)$, define its associativity coherence 2-cell to be multiplication by $\beta(g,h,k)$. Extend to arbitrary objects by direct sums. Since scalar multiplication commutes with every linear map, these components are natural and define an invertible modification.

On four homogeneous inputs, the monoidal 2-functor coherence equation compares the source pentagonator $\omega(g,h,k,l)$, the target pentagonator $\omega'(g,h,k,l)$, and the five triple-coherence components. Their ratio is $\beta(h,k,l)\beta(gh,k,l)^{-1}\beta(g,hk,l)\beta(g,h,kl)^{-1}\beta(g,h,k)=\delta\beta(g,h,k,l).$ Thus the coherence equation is precisely $\omega'=\omega\,\delta\beta$. Normalization gives the unit equations, and the same scalar identity on homogeneous summands gives the equation on all direct sums. The underlying functor is the identity, hence an equivalence; its inverse uses $\beta^{-1}$.

Conversely, in this gauge family the underlying functor, tensorator, and unitator are fixed as identities. Any normalized scalar triple-coherence modification is a normalized 3-cochain $\beta$, and its four-input coherence forces $\omega'/\omega=\delta\beta$ by step 2.1. Therefore $\omega$ can be untwisted by these data exactly when it is a coboundary, equivalently when $[\omega]=0$. This makes no claim about equivalences that change the grading group or the underlying 2-category.

citations.quote: For finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module categories $\mathcal M,\mathcal N$ over a fusion category over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic zero, the category $\operatorname{Fun}_{\mathcal C}(\mathcal M,\mathcal N)$ of module functors and module-natural transformations is finite semisimple. In addition, evaluation at the tensor unit identifies $\operatorname{Fun}_{\mathcal C}(\mathcal C,\mathcal C)$ with $\mathcal C$ and sends the identity module functor to $\mathbf1_{\mathcal C}$; hence the unit object of the monoidal $2$-category is simple. Here “finite semisimple” means a $k$-linear abelian category with finitely many simple isomorphism classes, finite dimensional Hom spaces, and every object a finite direct sum of simples.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and let $\mathcal M,\mathcal N$ be finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module categories. Every module functor $F:\mathcal M\to\mathcal N$ has left and right adjoints whose adjunction units and counits are module-natural. Every separable monad in the 2-category of finite semisimple $\mathcal C$-module categories has a separable splitting in that 2-category.

Here a separable monad is $(T,\mu,\eta)$ with a module-natural section $\sigma:T\to T^2$ of $\mu$ satisfying $T\mu\circ\sigma T=\sigma\circ\mu=\mu T\circ T\sigma$. A separable splitting means an adjunction $L\dashv U$ inducing this monad whose counit admits a module-natural section.

For a fixed fusion category $\mathcal C$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, there is a finite integer $R(\mathcal C)$ such that every indecomposable finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category has at most $R(\mathcal C)$ isomorphism classes of simple objects. More explicitly, write $I$ for its simple labels, $0$ for the unit, and $N_{ij}^k$ for its fusion coefficients. There are positive real numbers $d_i=d_{i^*}$, determined by these coefficients, with $d_0=1$ and $d_id_j=\sum_kN_{ij}^kd_k$. Put $D=\sum_i d_i^2$. One may take $R(\mathcal C)=\lfloor D\rfloor$. For every finite semisimple right module category, indecomposable or otherwise, the multiplicity $n_{ai}^b=[m_a\odot X_i:m_b]$ satisfies $n_{ai}^b\le D/d_i$. Consequently there are finitely many possible action multiplicity arrays at any specified rank, and finitely many indecomposable arrays at all ranks.

The real numbers used here concern the fusion ring, and are not categorical traces. No pivotal structure or positivity of categorical dimensions is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a fusion category $\mathcal C$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic zero. For each fixed possible rank of a finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category, its module structures are represented, after choosing action multiplicities, by a finite union of affine varieties of finite type. The change-of-basis group on each such variety has finitely many orbits, each open, if the degree-two normalized action-deformation cohomology vanishes at every point. This vanishing is supplied by [[lem-modc-module-deformation-complex-contracts]]. Orbits on a fixed labelled action skeleton are equivalence classes of its normalized module structures with that labelling; forgetting labels can only identify further classes. There are consequently finitely many module categories of any fixed rank and finitely many indecomposable finite semisimple module categories up to module equivalence.

The finite union over action multiplicity arrays is essential: rank alone does not specify an action functor. No algebra classification or categorical trace positivity is assumed.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided fusion category and let $\mathcal M\simeq\operatorname{Mod}^{l}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ and $\mathcal N\simeq\operatorname{Mod}^{l}_{\mathcal C}(B)$ be finite semisimple right module categories represented by separable algebras; the left-module notation is fixed in [[def-separable-algebra-and-bimodule-in-fusion-category]]. Their relative Deligne product as fixed in [[def-modc-relative-deligne-product]] exists, is finite semisimple, and is equivalent as a right $\mathcal C$-module category to $\operatorname{Mod}^{l}_{\mathcal C}(A\otimes B)$, where the algebra product uses the braiding $c_{B,A}$. This equivalence is independent, up to canonical equivalence, of the chosen algebra presentations and supplies the object tensor product in the separable-algebra model of $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C)$. The relative products assemble into a weak monoidal $2$-category: associators and unitors are the unique equivalences preserving the relevant universal balanced functors, the pentagon and triangle modifications obey their coherence equations, and the product is compatible with module functors and module-natural transformations.

For a separable algebra object $A$ in a braided fusion category $\mathcal C$, the object represented by $A$ in the separable-algebra/bimodule monoidal $2$-category has a left dual represented by the opposite algebra $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ of [[def-opposite-algebra-in-braided-fusion-category]]. There are evaluation $A^{\mathrm{op}}\otimes A\to\mathbf1$ and coevaluation $\mathbf1\to A\otimes A^{\mathrm{op}}$ bimodules, with invertible cusp $2$-morphisms identifying both snake composites with the respective regular bimodules. It also has a right dual represented by the positive opposite algebra $A^{\mathrm{op},+}$ with multiplication $m_Ac_{A,A}$; left and right opposites are not identified.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and let $\mathcal M$ be a finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category. There is a separable algebra object $A$ in $\mathcal C$ and a right $\mathcal C$-module equivalence $\mathcal M\simeq\operatorname{Mod}^{l}_{\mathcal C}(A)$, the category of left $A$-modules fixed in [[def-separable-algebra-and-bimodule-in-fusion-category]]. The construction below fixes the right-action/internal-Hom convention, gives the internal-end multiplication and a separability section, and proves full faithfulness and essential surjectivity. With these conventions, right module functors from left $A$-modules to left $B$-modules correspond to $B$-$A$ bimodules $Q$, acting by $Q\otimes_A-$; module-natural transformations correspond to bimodule maps.

A **fusion 2-category** is a finite semisimple linear 2-category with a weak monoidal structure, a simple monoidal unit, and left and right duals for every object. For a right dual $A^\#$ of $A$, the duality data include 1-morphisms
$$e_A:A\otimes A^\#\to I,\qquad i_A:I\to A^\#\otimes A,$$
and invertible cusp 2-morphisms from $(e_A\otimes A)\circ(A\otimes i_A)$ to $1_A$ and from $(A^\#\otimes e_A)\circ(i_A\otimes A^\#)$ to $1_{A^\#}$, with the associator and unitors inserted at the indicated sources and targets.

Here “simple unit” means that $1_I$ is a simple 1-morphism. A pivotal or spherical enhancement is extra structure: it requires its own duality coherence and trace axioms. Neither such enhancement nor a spherical trace is included in “fusion 2-category.”

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Composition of module functors is ordinary functor composition with the composite action comparison; its module equation follows by substituting the two module equations. Identities have identity comparison. Horizontal and vertical composition of module-natural transformations are their ordinary compositions and obey interchange because horizontal composition is a functor on the functor categories. Each hom category is finite semisimple by [F1]. The zero module category and finite direct sums of module categories are obtained componentwise; inclusions and projections are module functors. Their biproduct equations hold componentwise, and composition preserves these sums since every functor is linear. Both adjoints and all separable-monad splittings exist by [F2].

To identify simple objects, write the simple objects of a module category as $m_a$. Join $a$ to $b$ when $m_b$ is a summand of $m_a\odot X$ for a simple $X\in\mathcal C$. Rigidity makes this an undirected graph. Its components are precisely action-stable full semisimple summands, so indecomposability is connectedness. A natural endomorphism of the identity acts on $m_a$ as $t_a1_{m_a}$, because the field is algebraically closed and simple endomorphism rings are finite dimensional. Module-naturality and naturality along each summand inclusion force $t_a=t_b$ along every edge. Conversely scalars constant on components define module-natural endomorphisms. Thus the endomorphism algebra of the identity is one copy of the field for every component. In the semisimple hom category from [F1], an object is simple exactly when its endomorphism algebra is the field: decompose it into simples, whose endomorphism algebras are the field, and use the resulting product of matrix algebras. Hence nonzero simple objects of $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C)$ are exactly indecomposable module categories. By [F3] their ranks are bounded and only finitely many action multiplicity arrays occur; [F4] gives finitely many module equivalence classes for each array. There are consequently finitely many simple-object equivalence classes.

The universal relative products from [F5] supply the tensor pseudofunctor, its composition and identity comparisons, unit $\mathcal C$, associator and unit equivalences, and their coherence modifications. Its proofs establish naturality, the pentagon and triangle and interchange on transformations, so this is a weak monoidal structure on the same $2$-category of step 1.1. Under [F1], the identity of the regular module is the simple unit of $\mathcal C$; therefore the tensor unit is simple. Every object admits a separable algebra presentation by [F7]. The orientation is essential: an $A$-$B$ bimodule $X$, regarded as $A\to B$ in the algebra bicategory, acts on left modules by $X\otimes_B-:\operatorname{Mod}^l(B)\to\operatorname{Mod}^l(A)$. Thus Eilenberg–Watts identifies $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C)$ with the $1$-morphism-opposite of that algebra bicategory. Composing these functors identifies composition with balanced tensor, by the common balanced trilinear universal property. The product construction in [F5], evaluated on free modules and extended to their separability retracts, identifies tensoring these functors with tensoring their bimodules using the positive middle braid. Consequently this identification is monoidal with the stated reversal of $1$-morphisms. Fact [F6] supplies both left and right object duals there, with separate negative and positive opposite algebras. Reversing $1$-morphisms interchanges evaluation and coevaluation, so a left dual becomes a right dual and conversely; its invertible cusp maps become the corresponding inverse comparisons.
